intro.text: This entry describes rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a common chronic inflammatory joint disease with a complex, multifactorial genetic basis. Susceptibility has long been associated with HLA-DRB1 alleles in the major histocompatibility complex, and association studies have implicated variants at additional loci, including PTPN22, PADI4, NFKBIL1, and STAT4; a trans-ethnic genomewide meta-analysis brought the total number of RA risk loci to 101.

checks.explanation: The paper describes RA as a chronic inflammatory disease that destroys the synovial joints. It also includes RA among its 'seven common diseases' and 'common familial diseases of major public health importance'.

checks.explanation: The abstract treats HLA-DRB1 as the established RA susceptibility gene in the MHC, and its own analysis localizes one pathogenic gene to DRB1.

checks.explanation: The microsatellite study narrows the signal to a 70-kb region that contains NFKBIL1, but it names NFKBIL1 only as one of four candidate genes. The abstract reports no association of specific NFKBIL1 variants with RA.

paragraphs.text: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic systemic inflammatory disease of unknown etiology that primarily affects the synovial membranes of multiple joints and afflicts about 1% of the world population (Sakaguchi et al., 2003). Uncontrolled inflammation of synovial joints may cause progressive joint damage and long-term disability, and the disease is characterized by autoantibodies to immunoglobulins (rheumatoid factor) and to cyclic citrullinated peptides (anti-CCP antibodies) and by genetic associations with the class II region of the major histocompatibility complex (Barton et al., 2009). Approximately two-thirds of patients are seropositive for rheumatoid factor (RF) or anti-CCP autoantibodies (Stahl et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Yen et al. (2001) noted that RA is clinically heterogeneous with regard to progression of joint destruction, response to treatment, and involvement of extraarticular organs; homozygosity for disease-associated HLA-DRB1*04 alleles had been reported to predispose to major organ involvement such as Felty syndrome and rheumatoid vasculitis. They described rheumatoid vasculitis as a life-threatening extraarticular complication. Among Caucasian patients of Western European descent, they studied 30 patients with unequivocal rheumatoid vasculitis manifesting as ischemic mononeuritis, ischemic ulcerations, or peripheral gangrene, diagnosed by histomorphology or angiogram. A subset of RA patients has expanded populations of CD4+ T cells lacking surface CD28, and the highest frequencies of these cells are found in patients with rheumatoid vasculitis.

paragraphs.text: Hasstedt et al. (1994) studied 28 pedigrees ascertained through pairs of first-degree relatives with RA, in which RA was confirmed in 77 members and absence of disease verified in 261. Likelihood analysis assuming tight linkage to HLA supported an HLA-linked susceptibility locus with a susceptibility allele frequency of 2.16% and lifetime penetrance of 41% in male homozygotes and 48% in female homozygotes. Inheritance was recessive in males and nearly recessive in females. The inferred locus accounted for approximately one-half of familial RA but only approximately one-fifth of RA in the population.

paragraphs.text: Barton et al. (2001) investigated linkage to 5 human regions homologous to those identified in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. agent.process_note: Read every abstract-only paper in full and the opening and relevant sections of each full-text paper (WTCCC 2007 RA section and RA phenotype methods, Thomson 2007 first page, Yen 2001 methods and results, Vingsbo-Lundberg 1998 in full, plus the RA-specific passages of the CNV, eQTL, RPL23A, AFF3, 6q23, REL, GRAIL, Stahl and Okada papers), using Grep to find RA-specific statements. Six papers are title only (Gowans 1964, Burch 1964, Gregersen 1987, Feldmann 1996, Vyse and Todd 1996, Allcock 2001). Only the Gregersen 1987 and Allcock 2001 titles are cited, and only for what the titles say; I opened the Gowans 1964 title, but the other three title-only files were not opened. The papers do not establish a single causal gene. RA appears as a multifactorial disorder with many susceptibility loci, so the intro is descriptive rather than a number-sign statement, and the relationships are listed as MULTIFACTORIAL. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so no gene MIM numbers or locations are given. The only allelic variant listed is the PTPN22 R620W susceptibility allele. It is named R620W/rs2476601 only in Carlton 2005, Kallberg 2007, WTCCC 2007 and Thomson 2007; Begovich 2004 gives only 'a missense SNP'. Some HPO labels in the clinical synopsis are approximate (for example 'Autoimmunity' for female predominance), because no exact term was available.
